articles.summary: A jury is deliberating in the trial of the Massachusetts mother charged with murdering her three small children

blocks.text: Key moments in trial of Lindsay Clancy, the mother accused of murdering her three children
Watch: What is postpartum psychosis and why is it central in the Lindsay Clancy trial?
A jury is deliberating in the trial of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother charged with murdering her three small children at their home in suburban Boston.

In a case that has captivated the American public, Clancy has not disputed that she killed them, but her lawyers argue she should not be held legally responsible because she was suffering from severe mental illness.
Clancy is charged with three counts of first-degree murder in the January 2023 deaths. If convicted by a jury, she faces life in prison without parole.
Here are some of the most notable moments from the emotional five-week trial.
Defence argues Clancy had hallucinations and delusions

blocks.caption: Lindsay Clancy sits in court

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images

Prosecutors allege that on 24 January 2023, Clancy intentionally strangled all of her children - Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, eight months - with fitness bands in their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home before jumping from a second-floor window. Clancy, now 36, was paralysed by the fall and attended the trial in a wheelchair.

items: Lindsay Clancy's trial puts postpartum psychosis in the spotlight

blocks.text: Clancy's attorneys, while defending her, have never rejected her role in the killings.

Instead, they have put forth a defence of insanity, arguing that Clancy had hallucinations and delusions after giving birth to her youngest child. They pointed to treatment for mental health problems and that she checked herself into a psychiatric hospital just days before the deaths.

Prosecutors, meanwhile, have argued Clancy made a calculated decision to intentionally kill her children and should be held legally responsible. They allege that at the time, Clancy sent her husband, Patrick Clancy, out on errands so that he would not be home.
Clancy's family, including her former mother-in-law and husband, have testified about her mental state leading up to the deaths.

The five-week trial has sparked interest on social media as thousands watched the court proceedings. Hundreds of women have showed up outside the courthouse to support Clancy, wearing pink shirts with phrases like "She Needed Help" and "Peace For Lindsay".

blocks.caption: Women in pink shirts gather outside of Clancy's trial to support her

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
'A really hard time': Clancy's ex-husband takes stand
Over two days, Clancy's ex-husband, Patrick, told jurors about his ex-wife's declining mental health after giving birth and described the day his children died in gruesome detail.
He told jurors that Clancy's "big spiral" began about a month before their deaths.
"She started to lose a lot of weight, and she became very depressed, and she was having a really hard time," he said.
He described her intermittently seeking help from doctors and taking a variety of medications, adding that he recalled her saying she was starting to have thoughts of suicide.
Watch: Patrick Clancy recounts Lindsay's declining mental health before murders
Patrick Clancy described his last image of son Dawson sitting on the couch eating chicken nuggets before he left to get food and medication. He came back to find his children dead.
Lindsay Clancy sobbed in court as a recording of her husband's 911 call played. He can be heard screaming, "She killed the kids", after finding their children in the basement.

Since the beginning of the trial, conspiracy theories about Patrick Clancy have swirled online, including some speculating about his involvement. But he was never a suspect or under suspicion by investigators; Lindsay Clancy admitted to killing her children and her attorneys have not denied that.
Battles between lawyers and experts over Clancy's care
More than 10 expert witnesses testified for both the defence and the prosecution, including some who clashed with lawyers over Clancy's mental health.
Over the course of her treatment, Clancy was put on over a dozen medications, and sought help from a suicide hotline and the emergency room.

Clancy's team tried to convince jurors she had postpartum psychosis, a rare condition in which postpartum women can experience mania, depression or a mixture of both. Clancy claims she experienced hallucinations and delusions.
One day in the courtroom grew particularly heated as one of Clancy's psychiatrists, Jennifer Tufts, testified for the prosecution that Clancy did not show signs of psychosis during their sessions.
Watch: Clancy's defence clashes with expert witnesses
There were "no serious signs that her safety or anyone else's safety was at risk," said Tufts, who saw Clancy over a dozen times for five months.
But defence attorneys pointed to Tufts' medical notes, describing Clancy's "not hyper, pressured speech". Pressured speech - a rapid, frantic way of talking - can be a sign of mania.

Tufts denied that she believed Clancy had pressured speech, saying the "not" applied to both the words hyper and pressured. As defence attorney Kevin Reddington pressed her, she replied: "I don't care what it says. I know what I meant."
Reddington also grew tense as he repeatedly questioned another prosecution expert, psychiatrist Avram Mack, about whether postpartum psychosis is a diagnosis.
The American Psychiatric Association views postpartum psychosis as only a proposed illness, he said.
Mack avoided calling postpartum psychosis a recognised diagnosis, at one point responding: "I'm not sure if that specifically answers your question."
In a frustrated tone, Reddington responded: "I don't care."
Clancy's mother testifies
Watch: 'A very loving mother' - Lindsay Clancy's family testifies in murder trial
In addition to Patrick Clancy, Lindsay's former mother-in-law, her mother and her sister also testified, telling jurors about Clancy's deteriorating mental health after the birth of her son.
Lindsay Clancy was "begging for help", her former mother-in-law Susan Clancy testified.
"She had insomnia. She was losing her appetite," she said. "She was very anxious and sad."
She added that Clancy had been a "very nurturing" mother until the birth of her youngest son.
Clancy's mother, Paula Musgrove, said her daughter told her and her ex-husband that she was having thoughts of harming the children a month before their deaths.
Musgrove said her daughter was becoming paranoid and expressed that she thought her medications were "destroying her mind".
Clancy's sister Allison Ozga told the court that her sister was experiencing suicidal thoughts every day a month before she killed her children.
Judge tells jurors to disregard testimony about Catholic faith
Two days before closing arguments, Clancy's defence team requested a mistrial after prosecutors asked witnesses about her Catholic faith.

Prosecutors last week asked Clancy's former mother-in-law, Susan Clancy, whether she was aware that murder was considered a "mortal sin" after asking her if she was Catholic, testimony that the judge asked jurors to disregard.

Then, this week, forensic psychologist Kirk Heilbrun, who interviewed Lindsay Clancy after the killings, testified that he had asked Clancy whether suicide was considered a "mortal sin" while discussing her Catholic upbringing.
Judge William Sullivan denied Clancy's legal team's request for a mistrial, but told jurors it was an "absolutely inappropriate area of testimony".
"It is to be stricken. It is not to be considered. I can't be any more clear of that," he said.
With additional reporting from Ana Faguy and Brandon Drenon

If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide. www.befrienders.org.
In the UK a list of organisations that can help is available at bbc.co.uk/actionline.

articles.title: Allan Little: I met dangerously fanatical Mladić early in Bosnian war
articles.summary: BBC special correspondent Allan Little met the "Butcher of Bosnia" in the early months of the Bosnian war.

blocks.text: Bosnian Serb commander Ratko Mladić, dubbed the "Butcher of Bosnia" for his actions during the Balkan wars of the 1990s, has died in prison.
BBC special correspondent Allan Little was there throughout the breakup of the former Yugoslavia, and met Mladić in the early months of the Bosnian war.
At night, you could watch the fires of ethnic cleansing across the landscape. The flames provided the only light under the night sky and the black valley would glimmer with flecks of orange.

You could watch the men of our village move about silently in the shadows of their homes, each armed with some ancient weapon salvaged from wars long ago and, like the fears and the suspicions and the distrusts, handed down through the generations.
One morning I watched a procession of men and women emerge from a forest. They had been driven from their homes two days earlier and had fled with what they could carry.

Most were on foot. Some were crammed into the back of ancient farm vehicles drawn by donkeys. There were perhaps 40,000 of them. Their home town had fallen to a Serb advance that had come without warning.
Among them, one man seemed close to collapse. He stopped to speak to us.

The whole town had fled, he said. He had become separated from his wife in the long trek to safety and was now worried that she had not made it. His pale, almost translucently white skin was stretched across the bones of his face like parchment. His forehead was livid blue from a fall.
I asked him how old he was. He said he was 80. "May I ask" I said, "are you a Croat or a Muslim?"
The memory of it shames me even now as I hear, in my mind, his answer echo down the years.
"I am," he said, "a musician".

Our convenient ethnic shorthand reduced them to Serbs, Croats and Muslims. But they were also musicians and scientists and doctors and plumbers and farmers and mothers and fathers and brothers and sisters and very often children.

I met Mladić in that first hot summer of the war in Bosnia. We were at Lukavica barracks on the southern edge of Sarajevo. The barracks was awash with weapons and the menacing strut of the paramilitaries.
You could buy a Kalashnikov for 200 dollars, a hand grenade for just one dollar – the same price, I would soon learn, as the cost of a fresh egg in the besieged city.

I shook his hand and he held it fast and pulled me in close. He told me he had just come back from the Sarajevo city centre front line and I saw that he was pumped up by the exhilarating proximity of the fighting.

He held my hand for many minutes, fixed me with his eye and told me he was the great defender of brotherhood and unity in former Yugoslavia, and that he dreamed of a world in which there would no guns and no war. He struck me then as fanatical, dangerously so.

In the years that lay ahead, forces under his command committed the worst war crimes on European soil since the Nazis. They bequeathed to the lexicon of war a grim new euphemism - ethnic cleansing. They committed mass murder, extermination, mass rape, forced expulsions. They burned village after village, all in the name of creating an ethnically pure Serbian territory in Croatia and Serbia. Ultimately, at Srebrenica, they committed genocide.
Two days after I had met the old musician on that damp muddy roadside, I found myself drawn into the passions of the war in a personal and – at the time – devastating way.

My cameraman, Tihomir Tunukovic, a man I had known and worked alongside during the previous 18 months, was killed by a Serb gunner on a ridge above the road he was driving on. We had parted earlier that morning. He was 25 years old, a talented and ambitious young film maker from Zagreb.

We drove his body back along the rutted mountain pathways to the coastal city of Split. We broke our hearts at his funeral. The grief of it connected us to the sentiments of the war – the impulse to vengeance and counter vengeance – that were so much a feature of what we were witnessing.
General Mladić did not pull the trigger but his command created an atmosphere of wanton permissiveness which cost tens of thousands of lives.

articles.title: Jonvic Remulla urges Congress to merge BJMP, BuCor under DOJ
articles.summary: Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla on Thursday urged Congress to consider merging the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP) and the Bureau of Corrections (BuCor) under the Department of…

blocks.text: Published August 28, 2026 1:59am
Make this your preferred source to get more updates from this publisher on Google.

Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla on Thursday urged Congress to consider merging the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP) and the Bureau of Corrections (BuCor) under the Department of Justice (DOJ).
Under the current setup, the BJMP is attached to the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG), while the BuCor is under the DOJ.
“It is our position that the BJMP should be transferred under the Department of Justice, under the Bureau of Corrections,” Remulla said in the DILG’s budget hearing in the House of Representatives.
“I think it would be prudent for Congress to help us combine BuCor and BJMP into one facility since they perform the same jobs; basically they’re just mirroring each other,” he added.
Other Stories
Municipal and provincial jails could also be integrated, since they also operate independently, Remulla said.
Remulla was responding to ACT Teachers Party-list Rep. Antonio Tinio's concern that some detainees due for release have had their freedom delayed due to shoddy record-keeping.

Both the BJMP and the BuCor would have different case files for prisoners. The DILG secretary said combining two agencies would allow for more streamlined operations. This would also allow better record management for detainees. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Palace backs possible COA changes to confidential fund rules
articles.summary: Malacañang on Thursday said it sees a need to tighten existing rules on the use of confidential and intelligence funds to prevent officials from exploiting loopholes in the guidelines.

blocks.text: Published August 28, 2026 1:33am
Make this your preferred source to get more updates from this publisher on Google.
Malacañang on Thursday said it sees a need to tighten existing rules on the use of confidential and intelligence funds to prevent officials from exploiting loopholes in the guidelines.

Presidential Communications Undersecretary Claire Castro made the statement after the Commission on Audit (COA) said it plans to revisit existing rules governing confidential and intelligence funds, including provisions on acknowledgment receipts and the use of aliases.
Castro said Joint Memorandum Circular No. 2015-01 already provides guidelines on the handling and auditing of confidential funds.
She said officials who honestly account for the use of public funds should have no difficulty complying with the rules.
Other Stories
“Kung kayo naman po ay susunod sa polisiya at sa rules at wala naman kayong balak na magloko para sa pondo… hindi naman problema yung rules,” Castro said.
The problem, she added, arises when individuals deliberately find ways to circumvent existing regulations.
“Kaya kinakailangan pang amyendahan para hindi na makalusot ang mga panloloko,” she said.
Castro also maintained that existing rules already contain safeguards to protect the identities of confidential informants.
Under JMC 2015-01, she said, supporting documents may be placed in sealed envelopes and kept in an agency vault. These documents may be presented if questions arise during an audit.
Castro said COA also has a mandate to protect the identities of individuals whose information may be subject to an audit.
“So wala po tayo sa ngayon nakikita talaga na problema. Ang nakikita po nating problema ay yung mga tao pinapaikotan nga po ang rules,” she said.
She added that the Palace would await the specific amendments that COA intends to propose before commenting on their possible impact on government intelligence and confidential operations.

Confidential funds are currently in the news due to the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, who is accused of the misuse of the confidential funds allocated to the Office of the Vice President and the Department of Education. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Marcos sends condolences, offers prayers to Nepal flash floods victims
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Thursday expressed his condolences to the victims of the major floods and landslides that struck the Nepal-Tibet border. He also offered…

blocks.caption: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. (Photo from Bongbong Marcos / Facebook)

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Thursday expressed his condolences to the victims of the major floods and landslides that struck the Nepal-Tibet border.
He also offered prayers for strength of the calamity victims.
“The Philippines extends its deepest condolences to our friends in Nepal and to all those affected by the deadly flashflood yesterday,” Marcos said in his social media post.
“Our deepest sympathies go out to those who lost family, loved ones and friends. Please accept our most heartfelt prayers for strength in this difficult time,” he added.
The Nepal Tourism Board reported that one Filipino traveler was missing following a flash flood in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers in Nepal.
According to the tourism board, as of 2:45 p.m. Philippine time, preliminary records showed that 644 travelers had been reported missing in the affected area, including one Filipino.

Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said in a briefing earlier that the Department of Foreign Affairs and the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration were coordinating with officials in Nepal, as well as with the Filipino community, to determine the extent of the disaster’s impact on Filipinos. /apl

articles.title: Oil prices swing Alberta’s $9.4B deficit to $2B surplus, but finance minister urges caution
articles.summary: The same factor that's sent fuel prices soaring has created a massive turnaround for provincial government's budget.

blocks.text: Calgary
The same factor that's sent fuel prices soaring has created a massive turnaround for provincial government's budget.
'We cannot mistake a temporary windfall for a permanent trend': Jason Nixon
· CBC News
· Posted: Aug 27, 2026 1:13 PM EDT | Last Updated: 4 hours ago
Listen to this article
Estimated 6 minutes

blocks.caption: A pumpjack draws out oil from a well head near Calgary on Sept. 17, 2022. Alberta's revised surplus forecast assumes an ease in conflict and global oil supply squeeze, and for oil prices to decline substantially and average $73.50 US for the April-to-March fiscal year. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian…

blocks.text: Alberta's finance minister vowed to remain cautious while his government enjoys a massive budgetary turnaround due to high oil prices — an expected $2-billion surplus this year instead of the $9.4-billion deficit the province forecast a few months ago, just before war began with Iran.

Jason Nixon said he will not treat this dramatic upswing as a "blank cheque" to fund program spending, mindful that unexpected fossil-fuel geopolitics or the escalating U.S.-Canada trade war could create more damaging volatility.
"We know things can change and we cannot mistake a temporary windfall for a permanent trend," the minister told reporters Thursday.

Instead, Alberta will continue to budget conservatively and focus any potential new spending on relief for businesses affected by U.S. tariffs or Canadian counter-tariffs, or another round of "energy rebates" for Albertans, Nixon said as he updated his province's fiscal picture for the first time since Alberta tabled its budget in February.

items: Alberta premier doubles down on diplomacy with Americans to stave off U.S. tariffs

blocks.text: Back then, the province based its deficit-mired budget on a benchmark oil price it pegged at $60.50 US per barrel for the 2026-2027 fiscal year.

But that financial blueprint came out a mere two days before the U.S. and Israel began their attack on Iran, which led to a prolonged squeeze on oil tankers' access to the key Strait of Hormuz shipping route.
In the nearly five months since, oil prices have actually averaged about $88 US per barrel, the province estimates, which will substantially boost the province's energy royalties and tax revenues.
Alberta's revised surplus forecast assumes an ease in conflict and global oil supply squeeze, and for oil prices to decline substantially and average $73.50 US for the April-to-March fiscal year.
If that doesn't happen, and oil prices remain at or near current levels, Alberta could add several billion dollars more to its annual surplus.

But Nixon expressed a reluctance to take any such optimism to the bank, as a political veteran familiar with the extreme ups and downs of Alberta's budgetary volatility, heavily reliant as it is on oil prices.
"How can you not be in a good mood to stand up here and announce a $2-billion surplus and an over $11-billion swing in the fortunes of our province?" he said.
But he quickly added: "I know how quick it changes."

Rising oil prices lift not only the province's royalties from oil and gas extraction, but also its personal and corporate tax revenues. For every $1 US fluctuation in the per-barrel rate, the province's budgetary bottom line rises and falls by $680 million, according to Alberta Finance.
What this might mean for Albertans
The same geopolitical factor that's a boon to the provincial government has also sent gasoline and diesel prices skyward, worsening affordability woes for residents.
Alberta has declined to offer a break this year on its 13-cent-a-litre fuel tax, as the federal government has done and the province itself did in 2022 during a price shock.
Instead, the Danielle Smith government has offered the $100-per-adult Alberta Energy Rebate, "to get that money into Albertans' pockets" more directly, Nixon said.

However, far less of that rebate money than expected has reached those pockets. Only 1.2 million Albertans have applied for that direct payment out of 3.4 million eligible, which Nixon acknowledges is largely due to an onerous online application process.
The minister told reporters that for any future rebate programs, Alberta Finance will work with Canada Revenue Agency for better systems integration to smooth out the current application bumps.

The war-fuelled rise in oil prices also erased a previously $4.1-billion forecast deficit for the 2025-2026 fiscal year that ended in March, Nixon announced. His department is still finalizing the government's annual report and expects to have year-end figures available later this year.

Despite the newly forecast $2-billion surplus for 2026-2027, Nixon added that Alberta wouldn't actually have any money to direct into extra debt repayment or the long-term Heritage Savings Trust Fund, because of some complicated financial obligations and accounting rules.
The province reported that the government's taxpayer-supported debt sits at $94.8 billion. That figure is down $14.1 billon from February's budget, largely because of the oil price turnaround.
Alberta's oil estimates 'very conservative'
Alberta's revised forecast, which assumes oil prices will decline substantially this fiscal year, is "very conservative," said Servus Credit Union chief economist Charles St. Arnaud.
But he said it's difficult for the province to translate its budgetary turnaround into new spending, given how sensitive Alberta's budget is to volatility in oil prices.
“That mismatch is very hard, because if we start committing to new spending in the good years, when you have lower prices, that’s when you hit and have a deficit," said St. Arnaud.
"That’s a reason why they want to be relatively conservative in their estimates."
St. Arnaud added the province may not want to create expectations for a high surplus in its budget, to avoid the expectation of increased spending that could accompany it.
He also cautioned that Alberta's budgetary turnaround is possible due to it being less affected by tariffs as other provinces, which could change as Canada's trade war with the U.S. continues.

items: 'We will still feel it here': Tariffs might hit Alberta economy, jobs more indirectly, say experts

blocks.text: NDP calls for more support to counter cost of living

Alberta's surplus arriving as a result of increased oil prices is a sign that cost of living is still a problem around the province, NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi said. Affordability concerns are exacerbated by cuts to disability and seniors benefits, he added.

To support Albertans with affordability concerns, Nenshi called on the province to offer a break on the fuel tax, and use its sudden windfall to increase Heritage Fund savings and spend more on needed infrastructure like schools, hospitals, clinics or roads.

“There is an opportunity to use a windfall like this to catch up on capital projects, on one-time spending, as well as return money to people’s pockets, and save a little bit, because we may need it for a rainier day,” said Nenshi.

The Opposition leader also criticized how reliant the provincial economy is on royalty revenues, and said the UCP government needs a better plan to support Albertans facing an affordability crisis and to better diversify the economy.
“We should never be on a roller-coaster like this,” said Nenshi.
"When we get windfalls, we should know what to do with them, and we should be able to balance our budget without relying on Trump starting a war in Iran."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jason Markusoff is a CBC producer and writer. He analyzes what's happening — and what isn't happening, but probably should be — in Calgary, in Alberta and sometimes farther afield. He's covered Alberta for more than two decades, previously reporting for Maclean's magazine, Calgary Herald and Edmonton Journal. He appears regularly on Power and Politics, West of Centre and various other CBC current affairs shows. Reach him at jason.markusoff@cbc.ca

articles.title: Two killed in 'domestic violence incident' at school near Berlin
articles.summary: Police have arrested a 19-year-old male suspect after an incident in which two people were killed near the German capital.

blocks.text: Two people have been killed in a "domestic violence incident" at a school in the town of Gosen-Neu Zittau near the German capital Berlin, local police have said.
Brandenburg state police said they arrested a 19-year-old German man, who is "considered a prime suspect". They said it was not a "mass shooting", without specifying what weapon was used.
It is not yet known if the suspect was a student at the private Docemus school.
One of the dead was an 18-year-old secondary school female student and the other victim was a 30-year-old man who died when he tried to intervene, local media reported.
The arrested suspect is believed to be the ex-boyfriend of the 18-year-old victim, Maz Online reported.
Ulrike Liedtke, the speaker of Brandenburg's regional parliament, called the incident a "cowardly femicide".
"The fact that we once again had to witness deadly violence against a woman fills me with deep sorrow and anger.
"I am shaken that a citizen who showed moral courage and wanted to help also lost his life in this terrible act," Liedtke said.
State premier Dietmar Woidke said it was an "unimaginable act of violence".
The school's managing director Michael Kunz said classes will be cancelled on Friday.
Although there would be no regular classes, Kunz said the school would remain open for all students who wished to come.
"We want to provide them with a safe space where they can come together, talk to each other, and process what has happened," he said.
A "very careful" decision will be made in coming days about how school life will be structured, he added.
Last month in a separate attack, two girls were seriously wounded and a 16-year-old suspect arrested at a secondary school in southern Germany.

articles.title: What we should make of CIA boss's secret trip to Moscow
articles.summary: There is nothing routine about John Ratcliffe making a secret, 10,000-mile return dash to Moscow, writes Frank Gardner.

blocks.text: One US official told Politico that the "meeting was primarily to warn Russia against any escalatory action against the Baltic states".

The UK is also in Russian crosshairs. On Thursday, a foreign ministry spokeswoman said Russia could strike British military targets as retaliation for Ukrainian strikes on Russia using British missiles.
And a drone carrying an explosive which was discovered at an airport in the German city of Leipzig was probably Russian, security experts have said.
News of Ratcliffe's visit follows reports of US intelligence assessments that President Vladimir Putin was planning a limited assault on a Nato ally.

But you don't need the world's most powerful electronic eavesdropping organisation – the US National Security Agency – to know that Putin is under mounting domestic pressure to "do something" to break the deadlock.
Ukraine's deep strikes with long-range drones have not only hammered Russia's energy industry, they have brought the war home to ordinary Russians.

Nothing says things are not going to plan more than long queues for petrol and billowing smoke coming from stricken oil refineries. The Kremlin sees these attacks as Nato fighting an indirect war on Russia by using Ukraine as a proxy.
So how will Russia respond? There is a broad spectrum of possibilities here.

These include stepping up the ballistic missile attacks on Ukraine that Moscow is already launching, including targeting the centre of Kyiv, knowing that Ukraine is running dangerously low on Patriot interceptors to stop them.

Putin will be well aware of Donald Trump's periodic disdain for Nato and he may have calculated that a low-key attack on say, Lithuania, is not going to trigger Nato's mutual self-defence clause – Article 5 – and that the US will not respond.
In which case it would make sense for part of the CIA chief's unexplained mission to Moscow was to remind Russia that the US is still fully committed to Article 5.

Lithuania is of special interest to the Kremlin as it has a common border with Poland known as the "Suwalki Gap". Just 60 miles long, this strip of land is all that separates Russia's client state Belarus from its nuclear-armed exclave of Kaliningrad, which is separated from mainland Russia.
If Russia were to seize that it would effectively cut off those three Baltic states by land from their Nato neighbours.

Then there is the question of tactical nuclear warheads. It has long been said that Russian military doctrine views these small but highly destructive weapons as an integral part of its order of battle.
Moscow has been warned off, by friend and foe alike, not to break the 81-year long taboo on using nuclear weapons in anger.

Yet this could still be a tempting option for Vladimir Putin to "escalate to de-escalate" by demonstrating to Ukraine that it has such catastrophic weapons at its disposal it would be better for Kyiv to capitulate to Moscow's terms now or face annihilation.
Of course, in the absence of any clear, attributable, official confirmation from the US as to what this sudden CIA dash to Moscow was all about then it is always possible it was about something else.
That could be trying to persuade Russia to end its military cooperation with Iran, for example, or maybe about more prisoner swaps or the prospect of a mass mobilisation of Russian troops.
But make no mistake, this trip was highly unusual and it came at a time of rising tension between Moscow and the West. Something is almost certainly up.

blocks.text: Ratko Mladic, convicted of genocide for orchestrating the 1995 massacre of at least 8,000 Muslims in Europe's worst atrocity since the Second World War, has died.

Mladic died in UN custody on Thursday, his lawyer Dragan Ivetic said, without giving a cause. The former general had spent ​his last months in the hospital ward of the UN detention centre holding him in a suburb of The Hague, Ivetic added.

The slaughter in Srebrenica was the grisly culmination of a war that had lasted over three years, in which Mladic pounded the besieged capital Sarajevo daily with the artillery, tanks, mortars and heavy gunfire of his nationalist Serb army, killing 10,000 people.
The dead from Srebrenica were bulldozed into mass graves over four days in July 1995, some of them dug up and relocated to remote mountains so ‌as to hide evidence of the killings.

The goal, as determined by the United Nations International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY), was "ethnic cleansing" — the forcible expulsion of Bosnian Muslims, Croats and other non-Serbs to clear Bosnian lands for a Greater Serbia.
The tribunal found that Mladic, together with Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic and Bosnian Serb political leader Radovan Karadzic, were part of a criminal conspiracy to implement the plan.

"I do not recognize this court," Mladic, dubbed the "Butcher of Bosnia" by his opponents, said at an ICTY hearing on his case in 2014. When he was sentenced to life in prison in 2017 he shouted that it was "all lies."

blocks.caption: Bosnian Muslims carry coffins containing remains of 10 newly identified victims of the Srebrenica massacre, during a mass burial ceremony in Potocari, Bosnia on July 11. (Armin Durgut/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Karadzic, also convicted of genocide in 2016, and Mladic topped the ICTY wanted list for years ​after Western powers ended the war. But until Milosevic was toppled by a popular uprising in 2000, Mladic lived securely — if discreetly — in Belgrade.
Milosevic died in detention on March 11, 2006, ⁠a few months before a verdict in his four-year tribunal ⁠trial for genocide and other war crimes in Croatia, Bosnia and Kosovo.
Taunted peacekeepers

The army Mladic created to fight in Bosnia was a ‌model of ruthlessness. In some of the most horrific examples, prisoners suffocated in the heat after being forced to eat salt and denied water; were starved and raped in prison camps; were made to jump off a bridge and shot; and were gunned down at night by the hundreds after being driven out of detention with chemical gas.

"For me Mladic is a symbol of all horrible crimes that happened during the war — our girls were raped, and boys killed, only because they ⁠were Muslim," said Munira Subasic, whose son and husband were killed by Bosnian Serb forces after they overran Srebrenica.

Mladic had a cameraman film the blitz on the encircled enclave of Srebrenica, haranguing Dutch UN peacekeepers who misguidedly accepted his solemn word that the inhabitants would be safe in his hands. Srebrenica supposedly had "safe area" status, meant to protect civilians from ethnic cleansing.
"We give this town to the Serb ‌people as a gift," Mladic said to the camera, claiming the victory as revenge against Muslim Turks, who once held the area as part of the Ottoman Empire.
When NATO tried in 1995 to rein in his forces with the threat of limited airstrikes, his troops defiantly seized UN peacekeepers as human shields, chaining them to likely targets.

In November 1996 Mladic and top generals gave in to strong Western pressure that he step down as ordered by Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic, who succeeded ​Karadzic and was later jailed for her role in war crimes.
According to his son, Mladic was born in 1943, although official documents indicated a birthdate a year earlier.
He was an officer in the old communist Yugoslav People's Army (JNA) when Yugoslavia's disintegration began in 1991.

blocks.caption: A defaced mural depicting Mladic is shown in Belgrade on Thursday, with a Cyrillic inscription reading, 'Only God and no one else.' (Andrej Isakovic/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: When Bosnian Serbs rose in 1992 against Bosnia's Muslim-led secession, Mladic was picked to command ⁠the new Bosnian Serb army that swiftly overran 70 per cent of the landlocked country.

Dozens of towns were besieged with heavy weapons that once belonged to the JNA and villages were burned down as 22,000 troops of the UN Protection Force ⁠stood by more or less helplessly, with orders not to take sides.
A combination of Western pressure, covert American arms and training for Croats and Muslims gradually turned the tide against Mladic's army. Determined NATO strikes did the rest.
Despite Western appeals, ⁠the reformists ruling Serbia after Milosevic's fall did not dare move against a man who ​was a hero to a core of nationalist Serbs.

items: Mladic's conviction in UN court upheld

blocks.text: When he was ​finally arrested in 2011, he put up no resistance. His right arm ⁠was lame, the apparent result of an untreated stroke. He looked nothing like the burly general of the mid '90s.
He suffered a heart attack in 2013 and seemed older than his years. By his own account, he felt like a frail old man.
His appeal against conviction was rejected in 2021, as were repeated requests for his release on compassionate grounds, including in recent weeks.

articles.title: LTFRB summons PUV operators over Manila bridge crash
articles.summary: The operators of four public utility vehicles (PUVs) involved in a series of collisions in Manila have been summoned, the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) said Thursday.

blocks.text: Published August 28, 2026 12:44am
Make this your preferred source to get more updates from this publisher on Google.
The operators of four public utility vehicles (PUVs) involved in a series of collisions in Manila have been summoned, the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) said Thursday.
In a statement, the LTFRB said show cause orders (SCOs) were issued to the operators of the concerned PUVs.
The crash happened on August 25 along the Ramon Magsaysay Flyover, formerly known as Nagtahan Bridge, in Sta. Mesa, Manila.

According to the initial investigation, one of the jeepneys lost its brakes and rammed another passenger jeepney traveling ahead of it. The impact triggered a chain collision involving a motorcycle taxi and another vehicle, leaving 13 people hurt.
Other Stories
Acting LTFRB chairman Greg Pua Jr. said the operators were ordered to submit written and notarized explanations on why their franchises should not be suspended or canceled.

“We want to find out what happened, and one particular issue that we want to look into was the report of the police that the cause of this incident was a passenger jeepney that lost its brakes,” Pua said.
The operator of the jeepney allegedly responsible for the crash was ordered to submit documents related to the vehicle's registration, particularly those concerning its roadworthiness.
The operator is facing cases for allegedly employing a reckless driver and failing to provide safe and comfortable public transportation, the LTFRB said.
The same order was issued to the three other PUV operators involved in the incident.
Pua instructed the concerned insurance providers to immediately shoulder the hospital bills of the injured victims.
A hearing is set for September 10. —NB, GMA News

articles.title: How a glacier collapse may have caused Nepal-Tibet disaster
articles.summary: BANGKOK — A huge piece of ice that fell thousands of meters from a glacier into a river below may have unleashed the disaster in Nepal and Tibet that killed at least 180 people. Here is what…

blocks.caption: An aerial view shows houses lying deluged in sludge after flash floods at Devighat, Bidur Municipality, along the confluence of the Trishuli and Tadi rivers in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on August 27, 2026. Agence France-Presse

blocks.text: BANGKOK — A huge piece of ice that fell thousands of meters from a glacier into a river below may have unleashed the disaster in Nepal and Tibet that killed at least 180 people.
Here is what experts believe happened so far:
Glacier collapse
A glacier collapse in Nepal’s mountains near Tibet appears to have triggered the disaster.
“A large chunk of glacier fell from about 5,200 meters (about 17,000 feet)… into a valley,” said Simon Cox, principal scientist at New Zealand’s GNS Science.
It “transformed into this raging mass of debris… where it picks up rocks and sediment and trees and anything in the way and fires it on down through the canyon,” he told AFP.
The wall of water first impacted a border post, as documented in terrifying CCTV footage showing mud and debris engulfing the area as people fled before it.
It then travelled downstream into Nepal, flooding villages and bringing down bridges and buildings.
Seismic activity
The glacier collapse was large enough to register as a seismic event, initially mistaken for an earthquake.
But after further analysis, the US Geological Survey determined “that the seismic event was instead a glacial collapse and debris flow, and that no earthquake had occurred.
The collapse registered as a 5.2-magnitude “seismic event”, which took place at 8:37 am local time (0252 GMT).
Estimating just how much of the glacier collapsed will take time, Cox said, but it could range from “half a million cubic metres to tens of million cubic metres.”
Detective work
With the affected area largely inaccesible, experts are using satellite imagery and any available measurements on the ground to reconstruct the disaster.

“We can look at satellite imagery taken before and after the event, and try and see what has changed, essentially looking for what is missing from the mountains in the ‘after’ imagery,” said Lauren Vargo, a glaciologist at New Zealand’s Victoria University of Wellington.
Soon after the seismic activity was recorded, a nearby water monitoring station stopped transmitting, Nepali authorities said.
Stations downstream began going offline one by one, though water was registered reaching up to 12.3 metres high in Kalikhola, near the Tibet border at 2:14 pm, they added.
GLOFs
Early speculation suggested a glacial lake outburst flood, or GLOF, a growing risk as glaciers melt due to climate change.
A GLOF occurs when a fragile debris wall holding back a lake of glacier melt suddenly collapses, unleashing the water behind it.
Some experts suggested a GLOF might have been involved.
“Water does flow within glaciers and flows beneath glaciers,” said Adrian McCallum, a glaciologist at the University of the Sunshine Coast.
“But to my mind, the only reason why a large volume of water should all of a sudden flow down a valley is because it has been released,” he told AFP.

Other experts said they did not detect existing glacial lakes near the site of the glacier collapse, and theorised that water collected under the glacier might have cascaded down with the falling chunk.
The falling glacier ice could also have briefly dammed the river, collecting water behind it that was released when it dislodged.

Summer glacier melt upstream and monsoon rains would mean the rivers were already high, and the volume of water was also swelled by debris and mud picked up as it travelled kilometres from the initial collapse, added Cox.
Warnings
Nepali authorities first received word of a flood around 9:00 am local time, and began alerting areas along the Bhote Khoshi river to “stay on high alert and stay in safe areas”.
But is is unclear how many people received the warning, or how much time they would have had to respond.
“The reality is, if you are in a community underneath a large glacier and potentially a glacier lake where a GLOF could occur, then to some extent, it’s a ticking time bomb,” said McCallum.
And even for those receiving a warning, options would be limited, said Hatim Sharif, a hydrologist at the University of Texas San Antonio.
“Running will not help,” nor will trying to flee by vehicle, he told AFP, because the mud and water moving at high speed form a lethal combination “like liquid concrete.”
The only solution is to climb up a hill, at least 20 feet (six meters), he estimated.
Climate change
While it is hard to immediately attribute any individual glacial event to climate change, the warming planet is a constant background stress on these ancient ice rivers, expert say.

“The biggest way to mitigate the risk would be to reduce our greenhouse gas emissions to limit warming,” said Vargo. /dl

articles.title: Filipino traveler among hundreds missing in Nepal flash floods
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – A Filipino traveler remains missing following a flash flood in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers in Nepal on Wednesday evening, the Nepal Tourism Board said on Thursday.…

blocks.caption: An aerial view shows houses lying deluged in sludge after flash floods at Devighat, Bidur Municipality in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on August 27, 2026. Agence France-Presse

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – A Filipino traveler remains missing following a flash flood in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers in Nepal on Wednesday evening, the Nepal Tourism Board said on Thursday.
According to the tourism board, as of 2:45 p.m. Philippine time, its preliminary records showed that 644 travelers were reported missing in the affected area, including one Filipino.
Earlier, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro reported that there were no Filipino casualties in the flash flood as of Thursday morning, citing the Department of Foreign Affairs.
The board has yet to disclose any details about the Filipino tourist but noted that the information is still being verified and crosschecked with travel agencies and other local authorities.

“Following the devastating flash flood… Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation Government of Nepal, Nepal Tourism Board, Tourist Police and tourism stakeholders are working to verify the whereabouts and safety status of tourists or travelers who were at or travelling through the affected areas,” the Nepal Tourism Board said in a statement.
At least 165 deaths were reported after the flash flooding, and the riversides of the four affected districts were left severely damaged. /dl

articles.title: Nepali PM Balendra Shah heads to flood-hit Nuwakot to assess damage
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah left early Thursday for a field inspection of flood-hit areas in Bidur, Nuwakot. Minister for Infrastructure Development Sunil Lamsal is…

blocks.caption: Courtesy of Prime Minister’s Office

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah left early Thursday for a field inspection of flood-hit areas in Bidur, Nuwakot.
Minister for Infrastructure Development Sunil Lamsal is accompanying Shah on the visit.
According to the Prime Minister’s Secretariat, the team left Kathmandu by road at 9:30am for Bidur, one of the areas worst affected by the flooding.

During the visit, Shah and Lamsal will assess the physical damage firsthand and meet local officials, security agencies and elected representatives to discuss relief, rehabilitation and the restoration of disrupted infrastructure.
They are also expected to issue instructions to speed up the delivery of relief to affected communities and accelerate infrastructure reconstruction, the secretariat said.
Shah has been closely involved in the rescue and relief efforts since the flood entered the Bhotekoshi river from Tibet and caused damage downstream on Wednesday. /dl

articles.title: Optimus Prime and Eeyore voice actor Peter Cullen dies
articles.summary: Cullen voiced the heroic Optimus Prime in the Transformers TV series and then the Hollywood films.

blocks.text: His Optimus Prime voice was inspired by his older brother, a decorated US Marine and Vietnam War veteran, who suggested he should play the character as "a real hero, don't be a Hollywood hero".
"He said, 'Don't go yelling and screaming. He's strong enough to be gentle.'
"And that resonated with me, and I could hear his voice all the way to the audition. When he drops down, when he gets serious, is where I found Optimus Prime."
Cullen gave his brother a cut of the wages he received for playing Optimus Prime until his death.

The actor's performance as the character earned him a Daytime Emmy nomination for outstanding performer in an animated programme in 2011, and he was honoured with a lifetime achievement award at the Children's & Family Emmy Awards in 2023.

Cullen's other roles included Monterey Jack in Chip 'n Dale Rescue Rangers, and he voiced characters in 1980s and 90s animated series including Spider-Man, Donkey Kong, Alvin & the Chipmunks, Dungeons & Dragons, My Little Pony, Duck Tales and Gummi Bears.

articles.title: UP needs fresh funding for NOAH
articles.summary: The University of the Philippines is seeking fresh funding in the 2027 national budget for Project NOAH, the core component of the UP Resilience Institute responsible for developing hazard maps that…

blocks.text: The UPRI received P1 billion this week from the Department of Budget and Management for Project NOAH (Nationwide Operational Assessment of Hazards). It was earmarked in the 2026 budget after the government cut P255 billion from the Department of Public Works and Highways budget in the aftermath of the flood control scandal.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — The University of the Philippines is seeking fresh funding in the 2027 national budget for Project NOAH, the core component of the UP Resilience Institute responsible for developing hazard maps that policymakers and the public use to plan for weather events.

The UPRI received P1 billion this week from the Department of Budget and Management for Project NOAH (Nationwide Operational Assessment of Hazards). It was earmarked in the 2026 budget after the government cut P255 billion from the Department of Public Works and Highways budget in the aftermath of the flood control scandal.
The UPRI will use the mon- ey to upgrade its equipment, enhance hazard maps and fund research endeavors.
But the 2027 National Ex- penditure Program, for now, contains no new money for Project NOAH
The university pointed out that its funding in the 2026 budget was finalized only uring the bicameral conference committee.
UPRI executive director Mahar Lagmay said the P1 billion is “a good start,” but is not enough to execute all the plans they have in mind.
However, it’s a marked improvement from 2017 when NOAH was transferred to the UPRI.

Project NOAH had an annual budget of only over P30 million at the time, which it used to help cities craft their flood control master plans.With the huge increase in NOAH’s budget, Lagmay lai out the UPRI’s priority spending areas: high-resolution mapping of major river basins, support for the government’s Oplan Kontra Baha, simulation of major detention basins, drone surveys with state colleges and universities, native-tree mapping, sediment erosion and delivery assessment, mapping hidden waterways, promotion of nature-based solutions and artificial intel- ligence for disaster management.

articles.title: DepEd backs school safety bill amid shootings
articles.summary: Amid recent shooting incidents and other security concerns in schools, Education Secretary Sonny Angara yesterday expressed his support for the passage of the Comprehensive School Safety Act that…

blocks.text: This file photo shows a facade of the Department of Education.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — Amid recent shooting incidents and other security concerns in schools, Education Secretary Sonny Angara yesterday expressed his support for the passage of the Comprehensive School Safety Act that gives priority to school safety and well-being of learners.
The Department of Education (DepEd) said Angara showed his support to Sen. Bam Aquino at the Senate on Wednesday as the senator proposed the Comprehensive School Safety Act.
The bill seeks to institutionalize DepEd’s ongoing learner protection initiatives into permanent law, ensuring that critical safety protocols remain funded and sustained.
The legislative push follows nationwide concerns after shooting incidents at the San Jose National High School in Tacloban and the Ateneo de Zamboanga University.
The proposed Comprehensive School Safety Act establishes a three-pillar framework: prevention, response and recovery.
Under prevention, the bill mandates risk identification and safety training for parents, teachers and student leaders.
Response outlines emergency protocols, communication networks, active attack safety drills and coordination with authorities.
The recovery phase ensures psychosocial support, trauma-informed care and structured return-to-school plans.
The DepEd is expediting the recruitment of 10,000 school counselor associates nationwide, aiming to deploy them by year-end.
La Salle security
A student’s message on an online group chat with fellow students that he is a shooter disrupted classes at La Salle Greenhills in Mandaluyong City yesterday.

In a Facebook post, the school aid classes from preschool to Grade 12, including International Baccalaureate and Alternative Education programs, were conducted online as a precautionary measure. – Emmanuel Tupas

articles.title: Sweeping DPWH budget reforms set
articles.summary: There will be a sweeping overhaul in the budget submission process of the Department of Public Works and Highways, whose total project count for next year will be slashed by more than half, DPWH…

blocks.text: DPWH Secretary Vince Dizon also warned DPWH district engineers (DEs) that signing off on unvetted or “defective, anomalous” projects could land them in jail.
DPWH via Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — There will be a sweeping overhaul in the budget submission process of the Department of Public Works and Highways, whose total project count for next year will be slashed by more than half, DPWH Secretary Vince Dizon said yesterday.
Dizon also warned DPWH district engineers (DEs) that signing off on unvetted or “defective, anomalous” projects could land them in jail.

Highlighting a complete departure from “old budget habits” that allowed billions in public funds to be squandered on poorly planned infrastructure projects, Dizon said the DPWH is imposing a strict “no plan, no budget” policy across all regional and district offices.
“The old ways of budgeting are over,” he told reporters yesterday during his inspection of flood control and infrastructure projects at the EDSA Balintawak Cloverleaf area in Quezon City.

“We no longer accept project entries that consist of just a line-item title and a price tag. Projects must originate from community needs and satisfy complete prerequisite engineering requirements before entering the budget.”

Under the newly instituted accountability framework, DEs are required to personally sign certification documents guaranteeing that submitted projects have secured right-of-way acquisitions, detailed engineering designs and complete programs of work.
Dizon cautioned field officials against blindly approving lump-sum or unverified proposals, warning that their personal signatures will serve as primary evidence in criminal proceedings.

“If a DE signs off on a project and it turns out to be defective, anomalous, or ghost infrastructure, they are automatically held accountable,” he warned. “I will bring their signed certifications directly to the National Bureau of Investigation or the Ombudsman. It will be an open-and-shut case, and corrupt district engineers will go straight to prison.”

To enforce strict quality control and eliminate bloated, uncoordinated civil works, Dizon said the DPWH drastically pared down its project portfolio from 26,000 projects in previous budget cycles down to 11,000 highly targeted national projects.
Dizon reiterated that every approved project must carry written concurrence from the concerned local government unit to ensure alignment with local drainage and traffic master plans.
“While these reforms aren’t entirely foolproof, they create a formidable shield against the systemic corruption of the past,” Dizon added. “We will remain vigilant in guarding the public coffers.”

articles.title: P7.2 trillion budget bill for 2027 filed
articles.summary: The bill containing the government’s spending plan worth P7.2 trillion for fiscal year has been formally filed before the House of Representatives.

blocks.text: The bill serves as the legislative equivalent of the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP) that Malacañang annually submits to Congress.
Philstar.com / Irra Lising
MANILA, Philippines — The bill containing the government’s spending plan worth P7.2 trillion for fiscal year has been formally filed before the House of Representatives.
House committee on appropriations chairperson Mikaela Suansing said she has formally filed House Bill 10858 or the 2027 General Appropriations Bill.
The bill serves as the legislative equivalent of the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP) that Malacañang annually submits to Congress.
“We are working to ensure the careful scrutiny of the national budget for the year 2027,” Suansing said.
The House of Representatives started the committee-level budget deliberations last week.
After the committee, the bill will then be deliberated at the plenary.

The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) earlier said the Department of Education (P976 billion) and Department of Public Works and Highways (P644 billion) were among the agencies with the largest allocations in the proposed budget for next year.
Senate conducts budget hearing

The Senate yesterday led the Development Budget Coordination Committee (DBCC) hearing into the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027, with economic managers and senators talking about the need to tame inflation and end corruption following the flood control mess.

Monetary and fiscal managers from the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), Department of Finance, and DBM were grilled by the senators about the rising cost of living and the global headwinds – like regional wars and oil price shocks – that affect economic growth.

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian questioned BSP Governor Eli Remolona about the capacity of the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC), which Remolona chairs, in flagging suspicious bank flows due to corruption.

Sen. Francis Pangilinan pointed toAMLC’s failure to flag Syms Construction flood control contractorSally Santos’ transaction at Landbank in cashing out an alleged P457 million kickback to dismissed district engineer Brice Hernandez, a finding of last year’s explosive Blue Ribbon flood control inquiry.
Remolona and other BSP officials said the AMLC is undergoing an AI project to digitize its monitoring of millions of covered and suspicious transactions flagged by and reported to the council.
Sen. Panfilo Lacson said he led last year’s augmentation of P162.9 million for the AMLC budget in 2026 for this AI project.
Sen. Camille Villar raised concern over the decline in the country’s gross domestic product growth rate, from 2.8 percent in the first quarter to 2.3 percent in the second quarter.
Remolona said tight spending as a result of the flood control mess contributed to the economic slowdown.

Asked by Sen. Risa Hontiveros about the economic “have-nots” that contributed to the slowdown, Remolona said the country has to diversify its oil supply and to get into the AI sector, as he cited the Pax Silica manufacturing hub as a welcome initiative.

The Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) and the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration (OWWA) have asked lawmakers for an additional P4 billion for migrant worker assistance programs in the 2027 budget, citing the continuing Middle East conflict and the need to maintain sufficient resources for the repatriation and assistance of OFWs.
The 2027 NEP provides P7.726 billion for the DMW and P4.349 billion for OWWA. – Marc Jayson Cayabyab, Christine Boton

articles.title: How the Nepal flood unfolded over 10 hours
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — An initial technical assessment has found that the devastating flood that hit the Bhotekoshi river in Rasuwa on Wednesday entered Nepal as a major surge from Tibet. The flood then…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — An initial technical assessment has found that the devastating flood that hit the Bhotekoshi river in Rasuwa on Wednesday entered Nepal as a major surge from Tibet. The flood then traveled downstream through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers before reaching the Narayani river.

According to a technical report prepared by the Flood Forecasting Division of the Centre of Hydrology and Water Resources Research, authorities received information at 9:05am on that day that a major flood had entered the Bhotekoshi from the Tibetan side. The surge then moved downstream through the Bhotekoshi into the Trishuli river and gradually spread to downstream areas.

The division said it issued early warnings and alerts to people in the affected districts, river corridors and other high-risk settlements based on available river-level data, the flood’s movement and information received as the event unfolded.

The report says a magnitude 4.4 earthquake was recorded at 8:37am. About 13 minutes later, at 8:50am, the water-level monitoring station in Syabrubesi, Rasuwa, stopped transmitting data. Its last reading showed the river at 1.62 metres at 8:40am. The station’s warning level is 6 metres and its danger level is 9 meters, according to the report.

About 15 minutes later, authorities received information that a major flood had entered the Bhotekoshi river from Tibet. Between 9:15am and 9:16am, SMS alerts were sent to residents in riverbank areas of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Chitwan, urging them to remain on high alert. More than 600,000 messages were sent.
At 9:20am, the Betrawati water-level monitoring station also stopped transmitting data. Its last recorded river level was 3.55 metres.

By 10:28am, the flood was expected to reach the Dhading-Galchhi area and pass Muglin within a few hours. Authorities then sent further warnings to people along the Prithvi Highway, the Muglin-Narayanghat road and settlements along the Trishuli river.

At 11:26am, the river level at the Phurke (Malekhu) monitoring station had risen above the danger mark. Seventeen minutes later, at 11:43am, the flood swept away the Phurke river bridge and other structures. By 11:50am, floodwaters had reached the Malekhu area.

At 1pm, authorities received confirmation that the flood had already passed Muglin and urged people living along the river as far as Devghat to move to safer areas. The river level at Devghat reached 4.76 meters at 1:30pm. The initial estimate was that the main flood surge would reach Devghat at about 3:30pm, with the river level potentially rising to around 8 meters.
At 2:14pm, the water level at the Kalikhola monitoring station rose above the danger mark. The station recorded a peak level of 12.3 metres, according to the report.
By 3:20pm, the flood had reached the Narayani-Devghat area and the river level was still rising. At 4pm, the water level at Devghat peaked at 6.57 metres before beginning to fall.

By 6:30pm, the water level at Devghat had fallen back to about 4 meters. The initial technical assessment estimates that the flood brought an additional volume of about 20 million cubic meters of water, the report said.

From the earthquake recorded at 8:37am until the river level at Devghat began to recede at 6:30pm, the flood traveled from the Bhotekoshi through the Trishuli to Muglin, Malekhu and Devghat in roughly 10 hours.

articles.title: French Alps cable car accident leaves 23 injured
articles.summary: LYON, France — A cable car hit a crane in the French resort of Alpe d’Huez leaving 23 injured, three critically, officials said Thursday. There were about 50 people in the cabin of the…

blocks.caption: A man walks along a street of the French high-altitude resort of Les Deux Alpes, south-eastern France, on August 20, 2026. Agence France-Presse

blocks.text: LYON, France — A cable car hit a crane in the French resort of Alpe d’Huez leaving 23 injured, three critically, officials said Thursday.
There were about 50 people in the cabin of the cable car when the accident happened Wednesday morning at at altitude of 2,300 meters (7,500 feet), Alpe d’Huez mayor Jean-Yves Noyrey told AFP.
“There are mainly people in shock and cases of concussion,” Noyrey said, adding that he believed most of the injured had left hospital.
Cable cars are designed to stabilize themselves if they brake suddenly, but “on hitting the crane, the car tilted, and the people inside slid”, the mayor said.
“They thought they were going to die,” he added, “but the operator reacted well by reversing to level the cabin.”
The regional prefecture said there were 23 injured, with three in critical condition and 13 with severe injuries. /dl

articles.title: Norway’s King Harald, 89, in ‘extremely serious’ condition – palace
articles.summary: OSLO — The health of Norway’s 89-year-old King Harald, hospitalized with a blood disease, has deteriorated and he is in an “extremely serious” condition, the palace said…

blocks.caption: (L-R) King Harald V of Norway and Queen Sonja of Norway have taken seat at Oslo City Hall to attend the awarding of the 2024 Nobel Peace Prize on December 10, 2024. FILE PHOTO/Agence France-Presse

blocks.text: OSLO — The health of Norway’s 89-year-old King Harald, hospitalized with a blood disease, has deteriorated and he is in an “extremely serious” condition, the palace said Thursday.

Queen Sonja and Crown Prince Haakon, who is acting as regent during his father’s illness, have cancelled all royal engagements, said a palace statement. Norwegian media said they were at the king’s bedside.

Europe’s oldest reigning monarch has been in hospital in Oslo since August 17 suffering from hemolytic anemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of red blood cells which leads to fatigue and shortness of breath.
“His Majesty the King’s health condition is extremely serious,” it said, providing no other details.
The queen, Haakon and his wife Mette-Marit were all at the king’s bedside, with media showing them arriving at the hospital.
The monarch was admitted to Oslo University Hospital due to fluid retention from the cortisone treatment he was receiving.
Harald, who ascended the Norwegian throne in 1991, has had multiple health problems in recent years, forcing him to have a pacemaker fitted and to scale back his official schedule.
But he has always ruled out abdicating, arguing that he took a lifelong oath before the Norwegian parliament. /dl

articles.title: Desperate families search for missing after Nepal floods
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Anxious relatives crowded the corridors of a Kathmandu hospital Thursday as they searched for missing family after devastating floods on the Nepal-Tibet border killed at least 165…

blocks.caption: Local residents watch as a helicopter flies above houses lying deluged in sludge after flash floods at Devighat, Bidur Municipality in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on August 27, 2026. Nepal’s disaster agency said that 823 people remained out of contact on August 27, more than 24 hours after a deadly…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Anxious relatives crowded the corridors of a Kathmandu hospital Thursday as they searched for missing family after devastating floods on the Nepal-Tibet border killed at least 165 people.
Among them was Subash Khatani, scanning lists and speaking to officials in the hope of finding news of his elder brother, one of the hundreds unaccounted for after the disaster.
“My elder brother Ram Sharan Rasaili is among those missing in Rasuwa. That’s why we are out searching for him,” Khatani told AFP at the government-run Bir hospital in the capital.
On Wednesday, a tsunami-like wall of water and mud swept through villages and towns along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers, with Nepali police saying they had recovered 162 bodies.
Rasuwa in northern Nepal was the first district hit. But deaths were reported in seven districts as floodwaters surged more than 160 kilometres (100 miles) south to Chitwan, near the Indian border.

The cause of the disaster was not immediately clear, but the US Geological Survey said it was a glacial collapse that caused seismic activity and the “catastrophic” downstream impacts in Nepal and Tibet.
Chitra Bahadur Nepali was looking for his nephew Yubraj Sewak, a driver who had been travelling towards the worst-affected Rasuwa district before contact was lost.
“My nephew was on his way to Rasuwa and was in contact with my sister until about 8:00 am yesterday,” Nepali, 52, said, showing his photograph on his phone.
“We have not heard from him since the flood. His name is not on any of the lists we have seen, and another member of our family is also missing.”
As rescue teams scoured for survivors in the flood-ravaged districts, families moved between hospitals and police helpdesks, desperately hoping for word on those missing.
The Bir hospital said it would treat all victims for free and was “fully prepared” to handle the surge in patients, local media reported.

articles.title: From romantic getaway to hotbed of crime? Rumor mill fans Jeju fears
articles.summary: Jeju Island, South Korea’s traditional honeymoon destination, is facing an image crisis as a police scandal over allegedly mishandled missing-person cases fuels broader fears about safety on the…

blocks.caption: Police conduct a forensic examination after finding the body of Jang Mi-ran, who had been missing for several months, at a palm tree farm on Jeju Island, Monday. (Yonhap)

blocks.text: Jeju Island, South Korea’s traditional honeymoon destination, is facing an image crisis as a police scandal over allegedly mishandled missing-person cases fuels broader fears about safety on the island.
In just three days through Monday, four people who had been reported missing on Jeju were found dead, according to police.

Authorities have not linked the deaths or found evidence of widespread foul play. But the discoveries, which followed a large-scale search prompted by revelations that a police officer had falsely closed at least two missing-person cases, have shaken public confidence and fueled anxiety online.

At the center of the scandal is the case of Jang Mi-ran, a 37-year-old woman who disappeared after leaving her home in Hallim-eup, Jeju City, sometime between late May 12 and early May 13. Nearly three months later, a body believed to be hers was discovered Monday among palm trees less than a 10-minute walk from where she stayed.

blocks.caption: A police officer accused of falsely closing missing-person cases on Jeju Island is escorted out of Jeju Dongbu Police Station on Sunday. (Yonhap)

blocks.text: Jang’s case drew national attention after the police officer in charge allegedly closed it in May, falsely claiming that he had spoken with her.

Authorities found a man in his 60s who had been reported missing dead in Gujwa-eup on Saturday after a delayed search. His case, like Jang’s, had been falsely closed by the same police officer, news reports said.

The same day Jang’s remains were discovered, another person previously reported missing was discovered dead near a valley in Aewol-eup. The following day, a fisherman spotted the body of a man in his 70s in waters off Sinheung-ri, Jocheon-eup, and alerted emergency authorities.
Growing Jeju phobia

blocks.caption: A guesthouse on Jeju Island listed on accommodation booking platform Stayfolio (Stayfolio)

blocks.text: The concentration of cases, and the local police’s failures surrounding some of them, has unsettled residents and visitors alike.

“Many people come to Jeju to stay for several months at a time. I’ve heard that some tenants are canceling their leases following the recent incidents,” a Jeju resident surnamed Cho, who runs a short-term rental business, wrote on Instagram.

A recent Instagram post by Hong Hye-geol, a doctor specializing in preventive medicine and a television personality who has lived on the island for seven years, read, “When I cycle around Jeju, I often come across deserted roads in villages without even venturing deep into Hallasan. Stray just a little from a trail, and you can find yourself somewhere no one would hear you scream. I wouldn’t recommend either women or men going around here alone, even in broad daylight or on paved roads.”
Some even spoke of canceling trips to the resort island.

One Threads user wrote, “I was going to take my wedding photos in Gujwa because I’d heard it was quieter and had prettier fields than central Jeju, but I canceled. With everything that’s happened recently, I don’t think I’m overreacting.”

Another user called for a boycott, writing “We shouldn’t travel to Jeju until they get to the bottom of what the police officer did in Jang’s case and someone takes responsibility for the other missing-person cases.”
Although no clear drop in tourist numbers has emerged, tourism operators are growing concerned.

Bang, 52, who has run a women-only guesthouse in Jocheon-eup for eight years, said she has been receiving frequent calls from guests concerned about safety. Just two days ago, a group of three guests canceled their reservation, though it was unclear whether the recent missing-person cases had prompted the cancellation.

“The neighborhood is well lit, with streetlights and additional lights every 20 to 30 meters. We’ve always felt safe enough to leave the front gate unlocked while guests hang out in the common area before bed,” Bang told The Korea Herald.

“Catering exclusively to women used to be what set us apart, but now it seems to be making guests even more nervous. The police and local authorities need to step in before the baseless crime-related rumors surrounding the island create even more unnecessary fear.”
Tourism businesses in Jeju are particularly on edge as the island is already grappling with a decline in domestic visitors.

According to the Jeju Tourism Organization, 963,401 domestic travelers visited the island in July, down 12.4 percent, or 136,620, from 1,100,021 a year earlier. It marked the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic began in 2020 that Jeju’s monthly domestic visitor count fell below 1 million.
The downward trend continued into August. From Aug. 1-23, Jeju received an average of 35,295 domestic visitors per day, about 300 fewer than the 35,575 recorded during the same period last year.
